I recently posted a question to the list and received a couple of responses
to me personally. Thank you again to those that responded. It was
suggested that I post the replies, so I have pasted the origal question and
responses below. If you have further comments on this issue, please don't
hesitate to contact me or post to the list.

-------------------------
Original question:

I have conducted line transect surveys using distance bands for some
ongoing research. Each of the transects in the study was counted 4
times. Now, my question is essentially a data handling question. How
should the observations from multiple counts be managed before bringing
them into Distance? Should the data for individual species in each band be
summed, averaged, or perhaps take the maximum count of that species for an
individual band over the 4 separate counts? It would seem that summing
them would produce a problem in that you are almost certainly counting
individuals more than once.

-------------------------
Response #1:

The answer to your question about how to treat multiple counts on the same
transect depends upon the goal of your study: If the counts were relatively
close together in time, and you are interested in determining "average"
abundance during the count periods, then you should
pool the data from the 4 counts on each transect and multiply the transect
effort by 4. For example, if transect 1 is 10km long and the number of
observations for species A on each count is 0, 10, 2 and 5 then you would
enter data as if you had a transect of 40km with 17 observations on it.
If, on the other hand, you are interested in looking at trends in abundance
over time, you could enter each time period as a stratum and then estimate
abundance by stratum. You can investigate whether to fit a pooled detection
function over all 4 time periods, or a separate one for each time period.

I have heard of ornithologists who study migration using index methods
(e.g., simple counts) taking the maximum of their counts as an index of the
maximum migration density, but it seems a dubious practice to me. Perhaps
others have more experience in this area and can provide a justification
for when one may do it.

-------------------------
Response #2:

Perhaps keep them all as separate transects, and pool in DISTANCE?

-------------------------

> > -------------------------
> > Original question:
> >
> > I have conducted line transect surveys using distance bands for some
> > ongoing research. Each of the transects in the study was counted 4
> > times. Now, my question is essentially a data handling question. How
> > should the observations from multiple counts be managed before bringing
> > them into Distance? Should the data for individual species in each band be
> > summed, averaged, or perhaps take the maximum count of that species for an
> > individual band over the 4 separate counts? It would seem that summing
> > them would produce a problem in that you are almost certainly counting
> > individuals more than once.
> >

> > -------------------------

> > Response #2:
> >
> > Perhaps keep them all as separate transects, and pool in DISTANCE?
> >
> > -------------------------

Gregory, response #1 is fine. The above solution is wrong
though. Whether you use the analytic or bootstrap variance and confidence
interval options, Distance uses variation between transects to quantify
precision. This assumes that the transects are independent, which is not
the case when you walk the same transect 4 times. Hence you should
not enter the transect into Distance as if it was 4 different
transects. If the 4 counts were in 4 different years, the use of one
stratum for each year sidesteps this problem, because you estimate
abundance by stratum (year), so the encounter rate component of each
estimate is based on different data. (The detection function might be
pooled across years, but the analytic variance options are still valid for
this case.)

Bird people in highish latitudes often do several counts in one season,
because some species are more detectable early and others late. Then I
would select, species by species, which count or counts occurred at
suitable dates for surveying that species. (You might also want to
exclude late counts for species whose young have fledged, hence inflating
the abundance estimate.) If I selected more than one count for a given
species, I would then pool the data from the repeat counts, and multiply
the line length by the number of times I covered that line. e.g. if I
cover a line of length 5km 3 times, my effort is 15km. For point
transects, if I cover a given point 3 times, the effort is 3.
